promptText: In a Vision Transformer (ViT), how is a raw image converted into a form a transformer encoder can attend over?
options: The image is cut into fixed-size patches, each patch is flattened and linearly projected into an embedding, and a 2D-aware positional encoding is added before feeding the sequence into a standard transformer encoder
The image is passed through a CNN to extract a single feature vector, which is treated as one token
Each pixel becomes its own token, with RGB values used directly as the embedding
The image is converted to a text caption first, then tokenized like any other text input
explanation: ViT chops the image into fixed-size square patches, flattens and linearly projects each into an embedding of the same dimensionality as a text token, then adds 2D-aware positional encoding so the same self-attention mechanism used for text can process the resulting sequence.

promptText: Why does CLIP's contrastive pretraining (aligning image and text encoders into one shared embedding space) enable zero-shot image classification without any task-specific fine-tuning?
options: Because a category can be embedded as text through the same encoder space used for images, so classification becomes a similarity comparison against arbitrary candidate labels decided at inference time, not a fixed trained classification head
Because CLIP secretly contains a pretrained classifier for every possible object category
Because zero-shot classification only works on categories that appeared verbatim in CLIP's training captions
Because the image encoder alone is sufficient; the text encoder plays no role in classification
explanation: Since contrastive training generically aligned images and text (not to a fixed label set), you can embed any candidate text label at inference time and pick the closest match by cosine similarity, which is what makes the classification 'zero-shot.'

promptText: What is the key conceptual difference between multi-modal 'understanding' and multi-modal 'generation'?
options: Understanding models (like a ViT/CLIP-fused decoder) read an existing image and reason about or describe it; generation models (like diffusion models) start from noise and a text prompt and produce a novel image, with no mechanism to read an existing image and summarize it
They are the same technology under different marketing names
Generation models read existing images and improve their resolution; understanding models create new images
Understanding only applies to audio, while generation only applies to images
explanation: A diffusion model iteratively denoises random noise guided by a text embedding to create a new image; it does not take an existing image as input and answer questions about it, which is the understanding pathway's job.

promptText: An image is resized from 224x224 to 448x448 before being sent to a vision-capable model, keeping the same 16x16 patch size. What happens to the token (patch) count?
options: It roughly quadruples, since patch count scales with the square of the linear resolution increase
It roughly doubles, since patch count scales linearly with resolution
It stays the same, since the model automatically compresses larger images to a fixed token budget
It roughly halves, since fewer, larger patches are needed to cover a bigger image
explanation: Patch count equals (H/P) x (W/P); doubling both height and width doubles each factor, so the product (and therefore token count and cost) roughly quadruples.

promptText: In a speech-to-text-then-text-LLM pipeline for a voice assistant, what information is permanently lost at the transcript boundary?
options: Paralinguistic information such as tone, emphasis, hesitation, and background sound, since only the words themselves survive into the text transcript
The words the user actually said, since STT models are unreliable at word-level accuracy
Nothing is lost; a text transcript preserves all information present in the original audio
Only the language the user spoke in is lost, not the emotional content
explanation: Speech-to-text collapses the audio signal into words only; a natively audio-aware fused model can, in principle, retain tone, emphasis, and background sound that a plain transcript discards.

promptText: What is the job of the learned projection ('adapter' or 'connector') layer in a fused multi-modal LLM?
options: It maps the vision (or audio) encoder's output vectors into the exact dimensionality and distribution the language decoder expects, making them structurally interchangeable with text token embeddings
It compresses the entire image into a single scalar confidence score
It performs the actual patch-cutting step on the raw image before any encoder runs
It replaces the need for positional encoding on image patches
explanation: Since the vision encoder and language decoder are typically trained independently with different embedding spaces, the projection layer is the component that makes fusion possible by translating encoder output into decoder-compatible vectors.

promptText: How does a CLIP-style dual-encoder architecture fundamentally differ from a fused encoder-decoder architecture like GPT-4V or Claude's vision models?
options: A dual-encoder only measures similarity between separately encoded image and text embeddings and cannot generate free-form text about an image; a fused model projects encoder output directly into the decoder's token stream so one decoder can generate open-ended answers about the image
A dual-encoder is strictly more powerful because it uses two encoders instead of one
A fused model cannot be used for retrieval, while a dual-encoder cannot be used for classification
They are functionally identical; the only difference is inference latency
explanation: Dual-encoder models are ideal for fast similarity-based retrieval and classification but have no single decoder reasoning jointly over both modalities, while fusion architectures interleave projected vision tokens with text tokens so one decoder can answer open-ended questions.

promptText: What is the leading explanation for why vision-language models hallucinate objects or details that are not actually present in an image?
options: The decoder is still fundamentally a language-generation model whose strong language prior (learned from captions where certain objects co-occur predictably) can override weak or ambiguous visual evidence, filling gaps with plausible-sounding but incorrect content
The image patches are randomly shuffled before being fed to the decoder, so spatial information is always lost
Vision-language models have no training data at all involving real photographs
Hallucination only occurs when the image resolution exceeds the model's maximum supported resolution
explanation: The chapter identifies 'language-prior override' as the dominant hallucination hypothesis: the decoder's captioning-trained language prior can generate a plausible but unsupported claim (e.g., a knife block on a counter) rather than being strictly grounded in the actual pixels.

promptText: Why do vision-language models notoriously struggle with 'how many X are in this image' counting tasks even when they clearly recognize each individual object?
options: Attention is a soft, weighted mechanism with no architectural guarantee of discrete object individuation or an exact running tally, and training captions rarely state precise counts, giving little supervised signal for counting
Counting tasks are disabled by default in all vision-language model APIs for safety reasons
Vision transformers cannot process more than one object per image at all
Counting fails only when the image has fewer than four objects present
explanation: Counting requires exact, discrete enumeration, but soft attention over patches provides no built-in tallying mechanism, and natural captions ('a bowl of apples') rarely supervise the model to produce exact counts.

promptText: Why can't a Vision Transformer use the same 1D positional encoding scheme designed for text token sequences?
options: An image patch's location is inherently two-dimensional (row and column), and a 1D numbering scheme would lose genuine spatial adjacency information, such as which patches are vertically adjacent versus merely close in raster-scan order
1D positional encoding is computationally too expensive to apply to 196 patches
Text transformers never use positional encoding, so there is nothing to reuse
Image patches do not need positional encoding at all since self-attention infers position automatically
explanation: A naive 1D scheme numbering patches in raster-scan order would fail to represent true spatial adjacency (e.g., patches directly above/below each other), so ViT uses a 2D-aware positional scheme encoding row and column.

promptText: What tradeoff does 'image tiling' (splitting a large image into multiple sub-images before patch-encoding) introduce?
options: It preserves higher effective resolution and fine detail (like small text) that a single downscaled pass would lose, but multiplies token count roughly with the number of tiles, directly increasing cost
It reduces token cost by combining all tiles into a single averaged patch
It eliminates the need for positional encoding since each tile is processed independently
It has no effect on cost, only on latency
explanation: Tiling lets each region be seen at higher effective resolution within the encoder's fixed input size, improving detail capture, but a 4-tile image can cost roughly 4x the tokens of a single-tile version.

promptText: Why does Whisper sometimes produce fluent but fabricated text ('hallucinate') during periods of silence or non-speech noise?
options: Whisper's decoder is still a language-modeling component trained to always produce plausible text, and lacking a strong, reliably-trained 'no speech here' output class, it fills ambiguous encoder output with fluent but fabricated content
Whisper cannot process audio shorter than 30 seconds, so it pads silent gaps with random text
Silence causes a hardware buffer overflow that corrupts the output
Whisper only hallucinates when transcribing non-English audio
explanation: Since training data skewed toward audio that reliably contained speech, Whisper's decoder lacks a robust 'nothing to transcribe' signal, so its language-prior bias produces fluent but fabricated text on silent or noisy segments -- mitigated in production with voice-activity detection.

promptText: Why does CLIP-style contrastive pretraining typically require very large batch sizes (tens of thousands of examples), unlike typical fine-tuning workloads?
options: Each image's negatives are the other captions in the same batch, so a small batch provides only a few, often trivially easy negatives, while a large batch supplies many more (and often harder) negatives, forcing genuinely fine-grained discrimination
Large batches are required purely to reduce GPU memory fragmentation, with no effect on the training signal itself
CLIP does not actually require large batches; this is a common myth about contrastive learning
Large batches are needed because CLIP uses a recurrent architecture that cannot process examples in parallel otherwise
explanation: The batch itself functions as the negative-sampling mechanism in CLIP's N x N similarity grid -- larger batches expose the model to more numerous and more confusable negatives per step, producing a stronger training signal than a small batch's mostly-easy negatives.

promptText: How does the shift from a U-Net backbone to a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) backbone in modern text-to-image systems parallel an earlier development covered in this chapter's history section?
options: It mirrors ViT displacing CNNs for vision understanding: DiT patchifies the latent representation and applies self-attention instead of relying on convolution's local inductive bias, and empirically scales better with more data and compute, unifying the architecture with the rest of the chapter's 'sequence of vectors' theme
It mirrors Whisper displacing HMMs for speech recognition, since DiT also processes spectrograms directly
It mirrors CLIP's contrastive objective, since DiT also uses a dual-encoder contrastive loss instead of denoising
There is no meaningful parallel; DiT was developed completely independently of any vision-understanding architecture trend
explanation: Just as ViT proved attention could replace convolution for image understanding once enough data and compute were available, DiT replaces the U-Net's convolutional backbone with self-attention over patchified latents for image generation, and scales better as a result.

promptText: A team reuses their existing text-only RAG evaluation pipeline (Chapter 53's faithfulness/context-precision metrics with a text-only LLM judge) to grade a new multi-modal RAG system that answers questions about scanned document images. What is the critical flaw in this approach, and why?
options: The text-only judge is 'grading blind' -- it never sees the retrieved image itself, so it cannot verify whether a generated claim about the image's visual content is actually faithful, and will produce misleadingly confident scores regardless of true accuracy
There is no flaw; faithfulness and context-precision metrics are modality-agnostic by design and require no adaptation
The flaw is that text-only judges are always more accurate than image-aware judges, so this approach is actually preferable
The flaw is only that the judge model will run more slowly, not that its scores will be inaccurate
explanation: Faithfulness grading requires checking generated claims against the actual source; a text-only judge evaluating a description of an image it never received has no way to verify visual claims, producing confidently wrong scores -- the judge call must include the actual image.
